multimodal-encoder.name: Multimodal encoder
multimodal-encoder.definition: A model that maps more than one data modality into representations.
multimodal-encoder.explanation: The project uses separate linear towers because a four-pixel image and a caption vocabulary have different input structures. Each tower produces a two-number vector, and both vectors enter the same similarity calculation. Sharing an output space does not mean the encoders share parameters. Large systems use convolutional, transformer, or other pretrained towers, but the essential contract remains: compatible examples should be comparable after their modality-specific encoding.

embedding-normalization.name: Embedding normalization
embedding-normalization.definition: Rescaling a representation to have unit Euclidean length.
embedding-normalization.explanation: For a vector u, divide each component by the square root of the sum of squared components. The dot product of two unit vectors equals cosine similarity, so direction determines the raw similarity while magnitude cannot dominate it. Normalization needs a nonzero finite norm; the Rust project rejects zero and nonfinite embeddings. Unit length stabilizes the similarity convention but does not make the direction semantically correct without a useful learning objective and data.

contrastive-alignment.name: Contrastive alignment
contrastive-alignment.definition: Learning to score paired representations above mismatched ones.
contrastive-alignment.explanation: A batch of N image-caption pairs produces an N by N raw similarity matrix; division by positive temperature produces the logits used by cross-entropy. Diagonal cells are known pairs; off-diagonal cells act as negatives. Image-to-text cross-entropy asks each row to select its diagonal caption, while text-to-image cross-entropy asks each column to select its diagonal image. Averaging both directions trains both retrieval views. In-batch negatives are convenient, but a tiny or biased batch can make the task misleadingly easy.
